SportsTab.title: PSG on 'different level' - are they building greatest European dynasty?
SportsTab.text:
Some find success sweet but fleeting, others spend years building to the pinnacle, and then there are those whose lasting glory evolves into a dynasty.

After tearing Manchester City apart in large spells of their 4-2 Champions League victory on Wednesday, Paris St-Germain look well on track to join the latter bracket.

The back-to-back European champions sliced through City with astonishing ease to take a 3-0 lead into half-time, and were still able to score another despite a spirited second-half fightback from the Premier League leaders.

After obliterating Inter Milan 5-0 in the 2025 final before squeezing past Arsenal on penalties in last season's showpiece game, Luis Enrique's side are aiming to win a third consecutive European crown.

They would be the fifth team to do so going back to 1956, and just the second in the Champions League era.

"This PSG team are on a different level," Chris Sutton told BBC Radio 5 Live at half-time.

"They have just run all over Manchester City, who haven't been able to string passes together. It's been an absolute pummelling for Man City."

To mark PSG's latest display of attacking excellence, we're looking at how the Parisians compare to those clubs who have enjoyed the most dominant eras in European competition.

Some will point out that football existed before the European Champion Clubs' Cup began in 1955 - so apologies to Stan Cullis' 'world-champion' Wolves outfit and the Mitropa Cup's early Vienna heavyweights.

However, this top 10 debate is centred around winning European football's grandest prize.

Paris St-Germain 2025-present

OK, straight in with the current champions, because this is a dynasty in the making.

Paris St-Germain are hoping to enter that bracket and the 4-2 win against Manchester City on Wednesday reminded the rest of Europe why you shouldn't bet against them becoming continental champions for a third successive season.

PSG had a lacklustre start to the domestic season - they always do, don't they? - but boast an uncanny ability to click into gear when it matters.

In Manchester, Luis Enrique's side were at their unstoppable best. A ruthless blend of silky flicks and slick off-the-ball movement that saw a dazed City caught several frames behind.

"Unbelievable. PSG, what a team," Sutton said.

"PSG's press, I don't think there's another team that press with their intensity and ferocity.

"This [City] is one of the best teams in the Premier League getting an absolutely roasting. This is them [PSG] having a slow start to the season. Heaven help everyone."

The Parisians have been France's most dominant force since the arrival of Qatar Sports Investments 15 years ago, but it took a change of approach for the holy grail of continental success to arrive.

"It's the end of the glitter," professed president Nasser Al-Khelaifi after years of lavish spending, ushering out the "flashy, bling-bling" era.

Instead, Enrique arrived in 2023 intent on building a coherent team. There was still significant investment, but on younger players who could be moulded by his philosophy and discipline while given room to flourish.

The result was two scintillating Champions League triumphs.

SportsTab.title: Aston Villa: Champions League rout proves Villa are finding momentum
SportsTab.text:
Nicolas Jackson celebrated his first-half double by making a cutting motion which proved fitting on a night Aston Villa found their clinical edge.

A first win at Villa Park this season, three first-half goals with six in total and a commanding Champions League victory - all in the biggest European win in their history.

Unai Emery said his side had been impacted by the rebuild of the North Stand after three winless games at home this season but they showed no signs of struggle against Fenerbahce.

A dominant victory against the Turkish visitors leaves Villa already well placed to reach the Champions League knockout phase and will add to their slowly growing momentum.

Questions had been building as Villa picked up just one point from their opening three Premier League home games this season even if Saturday's 2-2 draw with Brentford ensured they avoided a third-straight home league defeat under Emery for the first time since February 2024.

Against Fenerbahce, they found a willing opponent. Scattered with former Premier League players, including Ederson, Nathan Ake, Romelu Lukaku and Nelson Semedo, the visitors would have been a formidable foe five years ago.

Instead, they folded quickly in the first half - despite Zion Suzuki's two important saves - as Johan Manzambi and Jackson's double put Villa in complete control.

The goals came in front of the skeleton of the North Stand, which will not have gone unnoticed as they had previously scored only once when attacking that end this season.

Ross Barkley's double and Tammy Abraham's late tap in added to the visitors' woes and underlined Villa's dominance.

They last scored so many in a 6-1 win over Brighton three years ago and had previously put five past Hibernian in the Europa Conference League in 2023.

The result provides another springboard and extends Villa's recent form to just one defeat in their last seven games.

However, Emery's rebuild will still take time. Before the international break, he described the opening five weeks of the campaign as similar to still being in pre-season with 10 new players to adapt following a chaotic summer of change.

Reflecting post match on how things are now progressing, he said: "They (Fenerbahce) didn't deserve 6-0 but for us it was very important how we achieved the first win at home and how we managed with different players, our progression and step forward.

"There is still a lot of work to do and we need time, we are progressively getting better and it was a good step forward. In the Champions League the three points are important. We want to be a protagonist in the Champions League.

"Now the clear objective is against Newcastle because of the lack of points in the Premier League."

The shoots of progress are already evident.

Manzambi glided past powerless Fenerbahce tackles, Ibraham Mbaye found space to exploit - even if he needs to improve - and Jackson was clinical.

Leon Goretzka made his debut as a late substitute and Suzuki remained commanding, continuing to slip into his role with ease.

"I think that's what Emery has been talking about with the potential of this team and what they can do," former Villa captain Stiliyan Petrov told TNT.

"There's been a lot of questions from the start of the season, even for this game as well. People asking how far they can go in this competition but it seems as though they're clicking together and there's a flow to their game.

"The players that Emery has brought in are starting to perform really well and it's a well-deserved win."

SportsTab.title: Red Roses: Amy Cokayne back as England prepare to face Canada
SportsTab.text:
England welcome back the experienced Amy Cokayne at hooker as their 41-match unbeaten run goes on the line against Rugby World Cup runners-up Canada in Toronto on Friday.

Cokayne has not played Test rugby since scoring the Red Roses' final try in a Grand Slam-sealing win over France in Bordeaux in May.

Saracens' Bryony Field, who has three caps to Cokayne's 94, drops to the bench after deputising impressively in the first half of the WXV Global Series last month.

During that part of the campaign, Canada ended England's near four-year winning streak with a nail-biting 26-26 draw at Sandy Park in Exeter.

Coach Kevin Rouet has targeted victory over the Red Roses as the main aim for Canada in 2026, with his team playing on home soil for the first time in more than 14 months.

Canada also play England in Ottawa on Friday, 23 October, with the two matches branded as the hosts' Rugby Rematch Tour.

The attendance for the Toronto match is expected to exceed 14,000, comfortably beating the previous record for a standalone women's rugby match in North America which was set when 11,453 watched Canada beat the United States in the most recent home match.

SportsTab.title: LIV golf: Organisation concerned by DP Tour's 'attempt to interfere' in player discussions
SportsTab.text:
LIV Golf has accused the DP World Tour of a "clear attempt to interfere" with its restructuring process, after the European tour said it would refuse membership to anyone playing on the breakaway circuit next season.

During a court hearing on Wednesday, the attorney representing LIV said that the organisation was "quite concerned" by the stance taken by the rival DP World Tour.

Rob Fitzgerald of Gibson Dunn, the attorney representing LIV, also said that the organisation would know by the end of the month if it could continue in a 'LIV 2.0' guise.

"We're continuing to monitor this situation very closely and we're quite concerned by it frankly," said Fitzgerald of the DP World Tour's position.

"The timing in particular strikes us as a clear attempt to interfere with our process with our players and potentially our reorganisation writ large.

"It also raises a lot of the same anti-competitive concerns that LIV has expressed previously regarding the way competing leagues have sought to box out and punish market participants, namely these players, from participating in LIV and really only LIV."

DP World Tour declined to comment on Fitzgerald's statement, but Guy Kinnings, its CEO, told BBC Sport on Monday that "players need to make a choice," toughening the organisation's policy on playing across the tours.

In previous years, conditional releases were struck with some top players - including Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton - enabling them to play on both the DP World Tour and LIV.

"Player freedom is the reason LIV Golf was created, and it's the foundation of LIV Golf 2.0, a league built around its players," Fitzgerald added as he continued his argument in court.

"LIV has been vocal in its belief in free agency and that the best players should have greater flexibility to compete across the ecosystem. It's unfortunate that another tour is taking an opposite view and pressuring our players with false choice."

Judge Michael B. Kaplan, overseeing proceedings in the New Jersey Bankruptcy Court, replied: "The comments I have read do raise concerns."

Responding to Kaplan's request for clarity on the timeline of LIV 2.0's creation, Fitzgerald said the "two critical pieces" were structural, relating to the investment from BC Partners, and having "sufficient number of players to have a bona fide golf league signed up by 25th of this month".

"We are working hard around the clock both on the player front and on the structural front," added Fitzgerald.

Asked when he would be able to advise the court "one way or the other" whether LIV was "toggling to a wind-down" or going forward, Fitzgerald said: "We would anticipate that decision will be made by the end of the month.

"Once we have full clarity on LIV 2.0, the debtors will need to very shortly begin making payments to host sites, vendors and other parties, so that we can schedule and prepare for LIV 2.0 events that we anticipate will take place shortly following the emergence."

LIV filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding.

As part of the court-supervised "restructuring process", which the organisation hopes to conclude in early 2027, player contracts have been "rejected" and no players are obligated to be part of LIV going forward.

During Wednesday's hearing, 19 player contracts - including those of Bryson DeChambeau and Dustin Johnson - were rejected, after having been adjourned from a hearing last week because those players wanted clarity that contract rejection would enable them to have conversations with third parties about their futures.

LIV recruited a number of high profile players following its launch in 2021, but now owes its participants at least $45m (£33m).

Current Race to Dubai leader Patrick Reed, who left LIV in January, has said he was accepted "from day one" after rejoining the European tour.

"This year fully playing on this tour only has been something I've really enjoyed and I feel like the guys have enjoyed having me come over and playing," said Reed.

"I don't feel any different. I feel like the guys have accepted me from day one.

"I can see how some of the guys would sit there and have an issue with guys coming over and just playing the big events.

"I've come over and played everything from big events, small events, events in the middle. I feel like it hasn't been any different for me."

Meanwhile, six-time major winner Rory McIlroy said that LIV was in "such a state of flux" and that the DP World Tour had been "more than accommodating" to the players seeking to leave the competition.

"The DP World Tour are well within their rights to change the rules and regulations," said McIlroy in his press conference prior to the Thursday start of the DP World India Championship.

"This is a way to protect their business and to make the tour as strong as possible."

SportsTab.title: Quickfire Doué and Dembélé inspire PSG to thrilling win at Manchester City
SportsTab.text:
A penny for Pep Guardiola’s thoughts. The legendary Manchester City manager was back at the Etihad Stadium for the first time since his departure at the end of last season and, well, the announcement of you-know-what.

Sporting a flat cap, Guardiola took his seat in the stands behind the City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, and the chief executive, Ferran “Not” Soriano, and, certainly, the TV director seemed intent on scrutinising him – if the number of cutaway shots to him were any guide.

Everybody knows where Guardiola stands on the great City scandal; the numerous guilty verdicts handed down to them on the 100-plus charges they have faced for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules. He has backed his former employers to somehow disprove them. But what did he make of his old team here against the might of the defending European champions, Paris Saint-Germain?

Not much in the first half would have been a reasonable conclusion. PSG played football from a higher plane and they might have led by more than the three unanswered goals they scored. But if defiance has been the theme for City – and it fed into Guardiola’s presence here – they produced plenty more of it during a thrilling second half.

City refused to accept the inevitable. They threw everything at PSG. Erling Haaland ran on adrenaline as City created a flurry of openings. The No 9 was unplayable at times; he finished with two goals and a few near misses. City were a goal away from worrying PSG.

The problem for them was the one that Maghnes Akliouche scored to put PSG 4-1 in front. It meant that City’s dream of an astonishing fightback was only an illusion. What a terrible concession it was for Gianluigi Donnarumma – and not for the first time.

It was a spin and blast from Akliouche on the edge of the area and Donnarumma appeared to have palmed the ball up and away. Except that it dropped all the way back down – quite a way back down – and into the net. How did it happen? It was one of many head-scratchers; the sheer weight of chances was difficult to process. PSG even threw in a late penalty fail by Ferran Torres, who came on as a substitute; his kick was weak and too close to Donnarumma. Are you missing it all, Pep?

City must play under a cloud, certainly until their appeal against the charges is completed, and they ran into a PSG team that shimmered with menace. Luis Enrique’s starting XI featured seven players who are on the 30-strong Ballon d’Or shortlist. The manager had another three from it among his substitutes, including João Neves and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

PSG bristled with their trademark assurance on the ball; the beautifully grooved combinations. It does not matter how tight the spaces are. They back themselves to get out of them. Witness the opening goal and a scintillating piece of team play that began deep on the right-hand side of their defensive third.

In the blink of an eye, PSG were surging up the flank and then opening out the move, Fabián Ruiz playing the final pass to Désiré Doué on the left. The winger cut inside and shot low for the near corner from outside the area. It was the precision that did for Donnarumma, although the former PSG goalkeeper had to do better at his post.

When PSG landed the follow-up punch just 75 seconds later, City were reeling, the home crowd stunned. It was a goal that featured two crosses, the first from Ousmane Dembélé out to Doué on the left. He took the ball down and crossed back for Dembélé, who stole in behind Marc Guéhi. The run was too cute, the header straightforward.

It was no exaggeration to say that PSG could have had five by the interval. City had no defence to their cut and thrust; the sheer pace of it, the positional fluidity too. Achraf Hakimi appeared to be playing almost anywhere but right-back. He popped up inside the six-yard box in the 32nd minute only to send a free header against the post, but City were swiftly disabused of the notion that the danger had passed.

PSG won the ball back and went for the jugular once again. Akliouche was involved, there was a lovely backheeled assist from Warren Zaïre-Emery and Vitinha lashed home a low drive. When Hakimi blew a one-on-one with Donnarumma on 39 minutes, it felt as though his team were toying with City.

Enzo Maresca made a triple change at the interval, introducing Matheus Nunes, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye – and the effect was immediate. City played with devil-may-care abandon. Their toothless first half was forgotten. Enzo Fernández blew a gilt-edged headed opportunity and Ndiaye worked Matvey Safonov before Haaland pulled one back. It was a whipped ball in from Ndiaye, which Haaland sent into the far corner with a flex of the neck muscles. He was not close in, either.

Could City take the lifeline? Antoine Semenyo ran through and dinked against the crossbar. The offside flag was raised, although he looked to have been level. City needed the next goal to make it interesting. Instead, they lost the initiative after another Donnarumma lapse.

It was the prompt for a whirlwind finale. Josko Gvardiol saw a header cleared off the line by Nuno Mendes, Fernández rattled the outside of a post and Haaland looped a header against the top of the crossbar before he scored again – a low finish after good work from Bouaddi. Haaland was denied the hat-trick when he stretched to prod at Nunes’ cross at goal – it was an excellent save by Safonov – and City finished with 27 shots and 52 touches in the opposition box. Those numbers would be enough for victory on most nights. Just not this one.

SportsTab.title: ‘I expect more’: the key questions from Martínez’s Manchester United broadside
SportsTab.text:
After Manchester United’s 2-0 loss at Atlético Madrid, Lisandro Martínez teed off at the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the rest of the executive. “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams,” said the defender. “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox] … Really poor [the Atlético defeat] – I have to control myself a lot but something is a reflection of the mirror of how our club is at the moment.” Here we consider the key questions emerging from Martínez’s explosive remarks.

Is Martínez’s view reflective of the squad generally?

Yes is the short answer. The Guardian has been told the decision to target three midfielders in Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba caused bemusement in the squad that no other areas were strengthened in the summer. Carrick led United to third last term after the side only had 17 league games remaining when he took over in January, having been eliminated from the other competitions. The need for defensive reinforcements is particularly acute because the back four of Diogo Dalot, Martínez, Harry Maguire and Luke Shaw has been together since 2022. Martínez is out of contract next summer and it is thought the 28-year-old may not be offered a new deal or have his one-year option triggered by the club, so teammates are conscious his outburst also came because he expects to leave.

How culpable is Wilcox?

As United’s director of football the 55-year-old wields near-unilateral power on football decisions, with only Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy, above him. If the buck stops with the executive, the most recent transfer window was Wilcox’s responsibility. This was the latest in a line of missteps on his United record. One concerns when Dan Ashworth (Wilcox’s predecessor) was on gardening leave from Newcastle in the first half of 2024, Wilcox interviewed potential replacements for Erik ten Hag before, oddly, deeming that the head coach should stay. The Dutchman signed a fresh contract but was sacked that autumn. Another involves Wilcox’s major falling out with the man he hired as the Dutchman’s successor, Ruben Amorim, after which the Portuguese said the director of football had told him he should change his favoured 3-4-3 shape. “I came here to be the manager of Manchester United – not to be the coach of Manchester United,” said Amorim, after a 1-1 draw at Leeds on 4 January (his job title was head coach). He was sacked the next day. Wilcox worked with Omar Berrada, United’s chief executive, at Manchester City, where Berrada rose to become chief football operations officer, and Wilcox became academy director. Wilcox moved to Southampton and became director of football from summer 2023 until April 2024, when he joined United, having been identified by Berrada, so there is scrutiny of his experience at elite level.

How much blame is Carrick’s?

The 45-year-old’s ability to prosper is related to the quality of Wilcox’s work, primarily in the market, so he cannot be solely responsible for a dire six points from six league games and two victories in all competitions all season. Yet by definition his role as head coach demands Carrick do the best with his resources, and that progress is made on the training ground. On matchdays there is scant excuse for United’s disjointedness, inferior running stats and inability, twice, to take advantage against 10 men: the 1-0 loss to City and Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham. How is Carrick viewed by his players? According to Santos they back him. “We believe in the manager, we believe in the whole staff, we believe in [ourselves as] players,” he said after the Atlético game. “We are in a bad moment but we have to work to change this result.”.

Is United’s unity and discipline crumbling?

For further evidence see Amad Diallo’s Snapchat post after the defeat by Atlético: “Fucking disgrace; I have no words.” So United have a World Cup-winner, Martínez, aiming shots at Wilcox and by implication Ratcliffe and Berrada, and a fellow senior player, Diallo, cursing but in ambiguous fashion, adding to the sense of meltdown at the club because it is unclear whether the “disgrace” meant the performance, Martínez’s diatribe, the squad his teammate referred to as not good enough, or something else. All of this is mirrored on the pitch, where United’s 671.4km run in the Premier League is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2 is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

Where are the Glazers in all this?

In mitigation Wilcox can point to the six American siblings, who remain majority owners and whose family has placed an eye-watering £1.1bn-plus debt on the club that severely restricts the transfer budget. Wilcox oversaw a £155m summer outlay and a net spend of about £100m in a summer when City’s corresponding figures were £457.5m and about £175m. City buying players such as Enzo Fernández (for a British record-equalling £125m), Elliot Anderson (£115m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£81m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£65m) showed their greater financial muscle, helped by being much better sellers of talent. How they have reached this point has, though, been thrown into sharp focus by last month’s verdict that they have serially cheated.

Are there positives for United?

Any straw should be clutched at so Carrick and his staff can view the first 97 minutes of Baleba’s United career as a rosy augury. After entering on 59 minutes against Spurs, a cute swivel and deft chip to Bruno Fernandes was a moment as impressive as the rest of his debut, and at Atlético the 22-year-old hunted down opponents and crunched into tackles, suggesting his game contains energy, muscularity and skill. It’s early days but perhaps if Baleba had been fit to start the campaign (he was recovering from an ankle problem) he might have affected one or more of the defeat at Hull, the 2-2 draw at Everton when Ainsley Maitland-Niles equalised late, the 1-0 loss to City when Phil Foden was sent off after 23 minutes or the Carabao Cup elimination by Brighton.

SportsTab.title: Finding Renée Richards: the complicated past and present of a trans sports pioneer
SportsTab.text:
It was a story that dominated tennis headlines back in 1977: Dr Renée Richards, an ophthalmologist who excelled as a male amateur player before a sex-change operation, was suing for the right to play in the women’s draw of the US Open. Where did Richards go for legal assistance? None other than Roy Cohn.

Better known for prosecuting suspected communists during the red scare and mentoring Donald Trump, Cohn turned his attention to fighting for Richards’s inclusion. His firm successfully argued the case – part of the narrative of a new biography, Finding Renée Richards: The Groundbreaking Story of Tennis’s Trans Pioneer by Julie Kliegman.

“The lawsuit was really significant,” Kliegman says. “Obviously, clearly, it was very significant for Renée. But the decision was limited to her, as opposed to setting a precedent for trans people going forward.”

For Kliegman – a sports journalist who is trans and non-binary – the project offered a chance to reexamine a 50-year-old cause célèbre and the topic of inclusion for trans people, in sports and in wider society, then and now.

“There are a lot of parallels,” Kliegman says. “What struck me the most is that if anything, the conversation and dynamics between athletes are amplified today by the hostility [that is] more powerful than anything Renée would have faced.”

Kliegman researched the story, in part, by accessing her subject’s multiple autobiographies as well as interview transcripts from another memoir project that never got published. They also interviewed Richards, now 92, in person multiple times. On one occasion, Richards showed Kliegman photo after photo of the celebrities who had posed with her over the years. Another time, the two met for lunch at the golf club where Richards still comes by regularly for a ladies’ day on the links.

These meetings also gave Kliegman a chance for some back-and-forth with their subject over trans rights.

“Renée today believes that trans women and girls should not be allowed to play girls and women’s sports unless they have not undergone so-called male puberty,” Kliegman says, describing this as a 180-degree shift from the lawsuit Richards filed in 1977. “She does not, overall, believe most trans athletes should be allowed to play girls and women’s sports. It was an interesting point of tension between me and Renée.”

Richards “cites research that shows trans girls and women may have an advantage over cisgender peers,” Kliegman says. “My impression is that the research isn’t conclusive enough.”

In writing the book, the author made a decision that went against their journalistic training but was in accordance with Richards’s wishes.

“In recent years, you usually don’t refer to someone by their former name, former pronouns, when they change it,” Kliegman says, “even when referring to past points of their life. I came to understand [using their birth name when talking about their early life] was really important for [Richards] to fully depict the back and forth, the push and pull, Dick [Richards was formerly called Richard Raskind] and Renée.”

The decision to use he/him pronouns in referring to Raskind, and she/her pronouns when it came to Richards, “was a tough one for me,” Kliegman says. “It goes against the journalistic norms I understand.” Yet, the author adds, “[Richards] felt I could not describe it accurately without ‘he’ and ‘her’ pronouns … So much in the book, Renée did not have any say over. It’s a journalistic project, not an authorized biography. Just about the only thing I think she needed a say over was [to] describe her respectfully.”

As the book tells it, Raskind grew up in a Jewish-American family in New York City. His father was an orthopedic surgeon, and his mother was a psychiatrist. According to the book, Raskind was bullied by his older sister, who made him wear her clothing. As he entered young adulthood, matriculating at Yale University, he voluntarily began wearing women’s clothing in private, and presenting as a female on visits to Greenwich Village. All the while, he played men’s tennis. After medical school at the University of Rochester, he became an ophthalmologist in New York, and joined the Navy, where he competed in service tennis tournaments and worked aboard submarines. Throughout college, med school and beyond, he dated women. Yet for a time, he discussed his conflict over his gender identity with several psychoanalysts.

“At the time, it was really, really difficult to get the care you needed as a trans person,” Kliegman says. “Also, on top of this, Renée was uncertain she was a woman. Certainly, she was a trans woman. Certainly, she was Renée. But there were also these other pressures encouraging her in the direction to present as Richard Raskind, whether it be for his career, for his love life, different forces.”

In the late 1960s, Raskind traveled to a clinic in Morocco that performed sex-change operations, yet decided against surgery. He subsequently met and married Barbara Mole, the woman who would become his wife and the mother of their son, Nicholas. After the marriage ended, Raskind decided to undergo a sex-change operation, this time in his home town of New York, in 1975. He chose the new first name Renée, French for “reborn”.

It was a new start in many ways: a new gender, a new name and a cross-country relocation to California. Yet Richards’s old love of tennis remained. She began competing as a woman, and having success.

“As Richard Raskind, he was a great tennis player,” Kliegman says. “He ranked as high as the top 10 in the eastern region of 35-and-over players. He was quite good, with a powerful lefty serve that people would talk about and recognize. Dick became Renée – and she remained a very good tennis player.”

Then she was outed – by broadcast journalist Richard Carlson, father of Tucker. With her background now public, Richards’s right to play women’s pro tennis was challenged by the United States Tennis Association (USTA). The organization questioned whether Richards was “genetically female”, as quoted in the book. Officials demanded a test to see whether Richards had “the conventional XX sex chromosomes”, according to the book. Eventually, Richards sued.

“Tennis is sort of the through line, one of the through lines of her life,” Kliegman says. “At any age, she could contribute to it … It sustained her through difficult times in her life. I think it’s what prompted the lawsuit – ‘Why I can’t I have this, this lifeline for me, a constant throughout my life, I should be able to play tennis, do the thing I love.’”

After a judge ruled in Richards’s favor, she was allowed to compete in the US Open. In singles, Richards lost in the first round to the defending Wimbledon champion, Virginia Wade. In doubles, Richards had more success, joining Betty Ann Stuart to reach the final, where they lost to Martina Navratilova and Betty Stöve.

The difficulties for Richards did not end. Some female competitors treated her with hostility. The book credits Billie Jean King with convincing most of the women’s tennis world to let Richards play.

“Billie Jean King was a huge part of Renée’s story,” Kliegman says. “She took a little while to make up her mind. She was quiet on the issue for so many years, but I understand why … She ended up calling doctors, asking them questions. She was not super familiar with the concept of trans people at the time.

“She also met with Renée, which I think was really crucial … It convinced [King] that [Richards] was a woman like any other, who deserved a place on the tour. Billie Jean King showed support by playing doubles alongside Renée … which was huge, I think.”

After retiring from professional tennis, she was ranked at No 20 in singles at her peak, Richards went on to coach Navratilova in what the book describes as a successful but sometimes bumpy partnership. Richards also returned to practicing ophthalmology for a long career, with a list of clients that included sports and politics journalist Keith Olbermann. There was a late-in-life tragedy for Richards: her son Nicholas died by suicide at age 47 in 2019.

“It’s still raw for her,” Kliegman says. “I don’t think the tragedy of losing a child is something most people ever get over.”

As Kliegman has gotten to know Richards, the author reflects that there is a little less daylight between their positions on trans rights, in part because of anti-trans policies of the Trump administration.

“If I did not see her views on trans athletes themselves evolve, what I did see was that she now understands restrictions on trans athletes … are connected to this broader project the right wing has to try to eliminate trans people from public life,” Kliegman says. “It’s not a distinction she was making, and was comfortable with, before Trump was reelected.”

TechnologyTab.title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
TechnologyTab.text:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".

Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."

A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.

The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.

ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.

Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.

ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.

These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.

He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".

Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white."

The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor.

Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples."

Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all".

"I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.

In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".

The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."

A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

TechnologyTab.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
TechnologyTab.text:
Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.

The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.

Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".

The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.

In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".

Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.

Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."

Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".

TechnologyTab.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
TechnologyTab.text:
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".

As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.

But, here's we do know so far.

The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).

Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.

Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".

The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.

Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.

Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.

But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.

On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.

A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.

The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.

When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.

In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".

It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

TechnologyTab.title: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire
TechnologyTab.text:
Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?

We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates, external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason.

But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?

Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager.

He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI.

"Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."

While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.

He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates.

"That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."

This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI "at some stages of the recruitment process".

According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.

However, it also found 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.

On top of this, the tech is helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market.

Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.

EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but decided to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.

Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process.

"What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."

Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible.

It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates.

But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews.

"A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script."

One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews.

While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would.

"I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"

According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.

And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI in the recruitment process, 29% plan to introduce it within the next year.

Hollie Moody says EDF does not currently use AI in its recruitment process but may have to in future.

For her, the use of AI in job applications remains a "moral dilemma" that employers and candidates will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits.

"It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."

TechnologyTab.title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
TechnologyTab.text:
"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating, external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation, external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Not yet, translators argue.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.

He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement.

"We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."

But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt.

"The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.

TechnologyTab.title: Bumble bought for $1.3bn in 'bet on the future of humanity'
TechnologyTab.text:
Dating app Bumble has been bought for $1.3bn (£980m) in what the new owners called "a bet on the future of humanity".

Investment firm Ithaca Holdings is taking over the loss-making firm and it directors, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will become co-chief executives of the company which once differentiated itself by having a "women-first" chat rule.

Bumble ditched the rule in August this year.

Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble's founder and current chief executive, said she would remain "actively involved" with the business she set up 12 years ago.

While it is unclear what Wolfe Herd's role at the dating app will be, she said she will work closely with the new owners.

Gupta and Hegeman said they wanted to use technology to "renew and accelerate businesses...in a world transformed by AI".

They said: "Technology should work in service of our deepest source of fulfillment, human connection and this investment is a bet on the future of humanity."

This contrasts with a recent debate over the safety of AI, with some experts claiming the speed of its development threatens the future of humanity.

Bumble's share price has soared as news of the deal began to emerge. The jump lifted its company valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after it floated the business on the Nasdaq stock index in 2021.

Since becoming a public company, it has made an annual pre-tax profit only once, in 2023.

In the following two years, it reported steep losses, though during that period Bumble had been working to incorporate new technology, including AI, into its app.

Its chief executive in 2024, Lidiane Jones, told the BBC she believed AI had "exciting potential" in dating apps related to safety, and Bumble had been looking at research that found Gen Z and milliennials were interested in AI assistance with creating profiles.

This year, the dating app unveiled several new AI features, including profile guidance to help people create dating profiles.

Bumble was launched in 2014 by Wolfe Herd who built the brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches.

It recently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals.

"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August.

Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates.

Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating.

Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services.

Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021.

According to a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier.

TechnologyTab.title: Phase Eight owner hit by cyber-attack as H&M probes separate hack claim
TechnologyTab.text:
The owner of high-end fashion brands Hobbs, Whistles and Phase Eight says it is investigating a cyber-security incident.

According to TFG London - the UK arm of retail conglomerate The Foschini Group - it identified an incident on Sunday affecting some IT systems and "specifically impacting our Phase Eight, Hobbs, and Whistles brands".

"We are actively investigating and working with external cyber security specialists," the company told BBC News in a statement.

Meanwhile, H&M is investigating a separate claim that it was attacked by a notorious hacking group.

TFG said its brands' stores are operating as normal but some website capabilities may be unavailable, adding "we apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate".

The retail group reportedly told customers in an email that it did not believe customers' payment information had been affected by the incident.

"As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted," it said.

The email, seen by news service PA, also said that those whose personal information had been impacted would be informed directly.

"We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time," it added.

Beverley Griffiths, senior lecturer in security and resilience at Bucks New University told PA that this was "a clear sign that major brands are firmly in the crosshairs of cyber attackers".

Fashion giants ranging from Adidas to Alexander McQueen have been targeted by cyber-criminals seeking to extort money by threatening to release customer data unless they are paid a ransom.

"No organisation is immune, so the real test of resilience is how quickly a business can detect an incident, respond and recover while keeping its customers informed," Griffiths said - adding customers should stay "vigilant" and wary of suspicious messages.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, said attacks targeting retailers were "starting to look rather like buses... you wait for one, and suddenly three come along at once".

She told the BBC that while it was too soon to ascertain how the incident affecting TFG London's systems occurred, or whether it was related to other recent hacks, "the retail industry has some serious questions to answer about how exposed its systems have become".

TechnologyTab.title: AI minister warns it is 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
TechnologyTab.text:
The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached.

Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June.

He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us".

Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents.

The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems.

He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."

In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe".

AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023.

But it was reported in September, external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed.

The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing.

Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation.

On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released".

He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported.

Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little".

"Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said.

"There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers."

The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems.

On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown.

However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.

Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules.

"We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said.

"What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer."

On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments".

"It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said.

TechnologyTab.title: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says
TechnologyTab.text:
Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.

Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.

His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.

But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."

Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology is a threat to humanity.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.

Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated.

"Let's get started today," he said.

He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.

He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology.

"We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."

Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute, external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute.

"In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."

Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.

Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".

However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU.

"In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said.

"When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived.

"Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."

TechnologyTab.title: King Charles warns malicious online actors are evolving their tactics
TechnologyTab.text:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

TechnologyTab.title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
TechnologyTab.text:
An artificial intelligence (AI) agent developed by Anthropic went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the 18 July tip was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation - but the force criticised the tech firm for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

It said the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.

Citing Anthropic, the police department said its AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites when it had sent the fake tip.

The company behind the Claude chatbot discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.

But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.

"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external.

"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."

The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.

But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide", the force said.

Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.

Organisations that had been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.

The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.

US President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will co-ordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers and religious groups.

Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, OpenAI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.

TechnologyTab.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
TechnologyTab.text:
It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.

It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.

The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.

But that is exactly what we have come to find.

After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.

I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.

"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."

It doesn't take long.

"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.

Three months after the fire first ignited, heat is still being detected beneath the ground.

We make our way towards the coordinates identified by the drone, and at first, there is almost nothing to see.

Then we feel it.

The soil is warm. A rock Pete picks up from the ground is, too.

Nearby, after scraping away a thin layer of earth, smoke begins to rise.

"It's really now cooking away," Pete says.

"Without the thermal technology we would be totally blind to this."

The wildfire began in the middle of July and burned across about 3,300 hectares – 33 sq km – of land, according to the Cairngorms National Park Authority.

At the height of the emergency, five experienced drone pilots were brought together to provide aerial information to the agencies fighting the fire.

Pete describes it as one of the most challenging environments he has ever flown in, with "multiple walls of flame", personnel and vehicles moving around the site and helicopters operating overhead.

Now the challenge is different.

The dramatic flames have disappeared, but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.

Each one found by the drones is reported to the land manager. They send teams who can dig into the ground and douse it with water.

For Ben Jones, senior site manager for the RSPB at Abernethy, knowing exactly where to send those teams has been crucial.

"We've been fighting this fire for over two months now and obviously we've got limited resources in terms of the number of people we have and we can't send everybody out everywhere all the time," he says.

"So we really need to know where these specific hot spots are - where we should be sending people - so that they can be as efficient as possible."

And despite the arrival of colder, wetter weather, the remaining fires cannot simply be ignored.

"Each of these hot spots has got the potential to reignite a larger fire," Ben says.

"Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says.

"It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet."

And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job.

Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape.

Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes.

"This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says.

There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread.

Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical.

"It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says.

Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot.

Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot.

Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil.

Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish.

Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning.

EntertainmentTab.title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
EntertainmentTab.text:
TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.

Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024.

"After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith.

"When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'."

The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after doctors had found a rare benign tumour, called a colloid cyst, in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work.

In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer.

She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner.

Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [the hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there.

"I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before."

A year ago, for the first time since the brain surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day.
